overview.title: Multi-input, multi-output models: the ticket-routing example
overview.section: 7.2 Different ways to build Keras models
overview.main_topic: A Functional model with three inputs (ticket title, body, tags) and two outputs (priority score, department), built with Input, Concatenate and Dense layers.
overview.central_idea: Most real models look like graphs, not lists. The Functional API expresses them directly: declare several Inputs, merge them with Concatenate, transform with a shared Dense layer, and branch into several output heads with different activations.
overview.importance: This is the first model in the book that Sequential cannot express. It establishes the multi-input/multi-output pattern reused in the following pages (training with lists or dicts, plotting, feature extraction).
learning_objectives: Describe the three inputs and two outputs of the ticket-routing model and their encodings.
Explain how Concatenate merges several symbolic tensors into one.
Explain why priority uses sigmoid and department uses softmax.
Read Listing 7.9 and compute the shapes of every tensor.

summary:
The page opens with the totals of the `my_functional_model` summary from p.220: **906 total params (3.54 KB)**, all trainable.

**Multi-input, multi-output models.** Unlike that toy model, *most deep learning models don't look like lists — they look like graphs*: they may have multiple inputs or multiple outputs, and this is where the Functional API *really shines*.

The running example is a system that **ranks customer support tickets by priority and routes them to the appropriate department**. It has **three inputs**:

- the ticket **title** (text),
- the ticket **text body** (text),
- user-added **tags** (categorical, assumed multi-hot encoded).

The text inputs are encoded as arrays of 1s and 0s of size `vocabulary_size` (text encoding is covered in chapter 14). And **two outputs**:

- a **priority score**, a scalar between 0 and 1 (**sigmoid** output),
- the **department** that should handle the ticket (a **softmax** over the set of departments).

**Listing 7.9** builds it in a few lines. With `vocabulary_size = 10000`, `num_tags = 100`, `num_departments = 4`, it declares three named `keras.Input`s (`title` and `text_body` of shape `(10000,)`, `tags` of shape `(100,)`); combines them into a single tensor with `layers.Concatenate()([title, text_body, tags])`; applies an intermediate `Dense(64, activation="relu", name="dense_features")` to *recombine input features into richer representations*; and defines two output heads on those shared features: `Dense(1, activation="sigmoid", name="priority")` and `Dense(num_departments, activation="softmax", name="department")`. The listing continues on the next page (p.222), where the model object is created from these inputs and outputs.

concepts.name: Multi-input, multi-output model
concepts.definition: A model fed by several distinct inputs and producing several distinct outputs.
concepts.intuition: Several sources of evidence merged into one understanding, then several questions answered from it.
concepts.technical: In the Functional API: several keras.Input objects, a merge layer such as Concatenate, shared layers, and several output layers passed to keras.Model.
concepts.significance: The typical shape of real models; impossible with Sequential.
concepts.example: Ticket model: inputs title, text_body, tags; outputs priority, department.
concepts.misconception: That multiple outputs require multiple models; one model can have several heads sharing features.

concepts.name: Concatenate layer
concepts.definition: A Keras layer that joins a list of tensors along an axis (by default the last).
concepts.intuition: Gluing feature vectors end to end.
concepts.technical: Concatenate()([a, b, c]) with shapes (None,10000), (None,10000), (None,100) gives (None, 20100).
concepts.significance: The merge point that turns three inputs into one feature tensor.
concepts.misconception: That Concatenate adds the vectors element-wise; it stacks them, increasing the dimension.

concepts.name: Multi-hot encoding
concepts.definition: Binary vector with 1s at the indices of all categories/words present.
concepts.intuition: A checklist of which vocabulary items occur.
concepts.technical: Size = vocabulary_size (10,000) for text, num_tags (100) for tags here.
concepts.significance: Gives fixed-size inputs suitable for Dense layers.
concepts.example: Tags {billing, urgent} → 1s at those two positions out of 100.
concepts.misconception: That it preserves word order; it doesn't.

code.title: A multi-input, multi-output Functional model (first part; continues on p.222)
code.original_code:
vocabulary_size = 10000
num_tags = 100
num_departments = 4

title = keras.Input(shape=(vocabulary_size,), name="title")
text_body = keras.Input(shape=(vocabulary_size,), name="text_body")
tags = keras.Input(shape=(num_tags,), name="tags")

features = layers.Concatenate()([title, text_body, tags])
features = layers.Dense(64, activation="relu", name="dense_features")(features)

priority = layers.Dense(1, activation="sigmoid", name="priority")(features)
department = layers.Dense(
    num_departments, activation="softmax", name="department"
)(features)
code.what_it_does: Declares three named inputs, concatenates them, applies a shared 64-unit relu layer, and defines two output heads: a sigmoid priority score and a softmax department classifier. The model object itself is created in the part of the listing on p.222.

line_explanations.explanation: Callout: defines model inputs. Three named Inputs of shapes (10000,), (10000,), (100,).
Callout: combines input features into a single tensor, features, by concatenating them → (None, 20100).
Callout: applies an intermediate layer to recombine input features into richer representations → (None, 64).
Callout: defines model outputs. priority (None, 1) with sigmoid; department (None, 4) with softmax.

code.inputs_outputs: Symbolic inputs title, text_body, tags; symbolic outputs priority (None, 1) and department (None, 4).
code.theory_link: Multi-task learning with shared features; sigmoid for a bounded score, softmax for single-label classification.

deeper.title: Tensor shapes through Listing 7.9
deeper.body:
AI explanation using the listing's constants:
1. `title`: `(None, 10000)`; `text_body`: `(None, 10000)`; `tags`: `(None, 100)`.
2. `Concatenate()` along the last axis: `(None, 20100)`.
3. `dense_features`: `(None, 64)`, with $20100\times64+64 = 1{,}286{,}464$ parameters.
4. `priority`: `(None, 1)`, 65 parameters.
5. `department`: `(None, 4)`, 260 parameters.

deeper.title: Why one shared trunk with two heads?
deeper.body: Beyond the book: priority and department are related judgments about the same ticket (an outage report is both urgent and for engineering). Sharing `dense_features` lets both tasks shape a common representation and needs fewer parameters than two separate models — the idea behind multi-task learning.

takeaways: Most real models are graphs; the Functional API shines for multiple inputs and outputs.
The ticket model has three inputs (title, body, tags) and two outputs (priority, department).
Text and tags are multi-hot encoded; vocabulary_size = 10000, num_tags = 100.
Concatenate merges inputs into one feature tensor; a shared Dense(64, relu) recombines them.
priority uses a 1-unit sigmoid head; department a 4-unit softmax head.
Naming inputs and output layers will let you pass data by name.

questions.question: What is the output shape of layers.Concatenate()([title, text_body, tags]) in Listing 7.9?
questions.explanation: Concatenation along the last axis adds dimensions: 10000 + 10000 + 100. (None, 10000) ignores two inputs; (None, 3, 10000) would be stacking (and tags has a different size); (None, 64) is after the Dense layer.

questions.question: Why does the priority head use sigmoid and the department head softmax?
questions.answer: Priority is a single scalar between 0 and 1, which sigmoid produces; department is one choice among several departments, so softmax gives a probability distribution over them.
questions.explanation: From the two output bullets on the page.

Why couldn't this model be built with keras.Sequential?
questions.answer: It has three inputs merged by Concatenate and two outputs branching from shared features; Sequential supports only one input, one output and a linear chain.
